A1.justification: Both PDFs describe PhysGM and PhysAssets. The complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching retained supplementary figures across renumbering. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent identifying the substantive revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation results, CLIP similarity and human-preference comparisons in Table 1, a DPO ablation, and qualitative experiments in the main text and supplement.

after.justification: v2 reports simulation comparisons and DPO results, revised human-preference outcomes, and additional original reconstruction results on GSO in Table 2 and Figure 9.

M1.justification: v1 uses MVDream, an LGM-initialized U-Net and probabilistic appearance and physics prediction. v2 replaces these with MVAdapter, DINOv3 and camera encoders, a 24-layer transformer and a DPT Gaussian decoder. It replaces probabilistic appearance prediction with direct Gaussian prediction, restricts continuous physics prediction to Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio, adds alpha and LPIPS reconstruction losses, and fine-tunes only physics heads during DPO instead of both prediction heads.

E1.justification: v2 adds a dedicated four-view-to-novel-view reconstruction evaluation on GSO alongside dynamic simulation, introduces HSSD assets into training, and reports broader material coverage: 46 categories versus v1's 17-material annotation vocabulary, although v2 elsewhere says 45. GSO itself was already included in v1's asset collection. Stretching, dropping, complex backgrounds and multi-object interactions were already evaluated in v1's appendix.

E2.justification: LGM and GS-LRM become quantitative reconstruction comparators in v2 Table 2; v1 cited them but did not report this comparison. Table 1 retains OmniPhysGS, DreamPhysics and the no-DPO variant. v2 Appendix A.4 instead names PhysGaussian, OmniPhysGS and DreamGaussian4D as user-study comparators, conflicting with Table 1, so those purported comparator substitutions cannot be reliably established.

E3.justification: The user study changes from pairwise 2AFC to 4AFC. Reported training changes from 8 A800 GPUs for 12 hours to 32 for three days, with learning rate changing from 1e-6 to 2e-4 and gradient clipping from 1 to 10. PhysAssets expands from 24,000+ objects to a reported 49,206 training and 1,009 held-out GSO objects. New reconstruction evaluation specifies four input views, eight novel target views, and PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS. Annotation changes from four-view SigLIP-2 to eight-view Qwen3-VL.

E4.justification: v2 Appendix D.2.2 adds qualitative prompt-sensitivity findings: detailed constraints can produce inconsistent generation, while strict identity and orientation constraints can yield unrealistic motion. The DPO ablation remains, with revised human-preference evidence but unchanged CLIP scores and retained visual examples. The extensive physical-interaction and complex-background demonstrations are inherited from v1, rather than new robustness tests.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run counts, random seeds, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests for its experimental results. v2's participant counts and response-filtering details expand the user-study protocol, but do not introduce uncertainty estimation. Predicted physical-parameter distributions are model components rather than experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 1 retains every CLIP similarity value but replaces the pairwise preference results with four-way shares, including 42.8% for the full model; these are not directly comparable across versions. New Table 2 reports reconstruction results: at 256 resolution, PhysGM versus LGM achieves PSNR 25.47 versus 21.44; at 512, PhysGM versus GS-LRM achieves lower PSNR, 28.95 versus 30.52, but better SSIM and LPIPS. New material-distribution statistics and reconstruction visualizations add further results.

T1.justification: v2 removes v1's explicit probabilistic appearance formulation and adds mathematical definitions for bounding-box normalization, landing-frame detection and temporally aligned trajectory comparison in Appendix D.2.4. These extend the formal specification beyond v1's brief trajectory-distance description. The MPM update equations, three constitutive models and DPO objective remain essentially unchanged; neither version provides theoretical guarantees or proofs.

C1.justification: The central claims of feed-forward physical Gaussian prediction, two-stage DPO training and approximately one-minute synthesis remain. v2 adds an explicit argument that joint reconstruction and physics prediction exploits physical cues in appearance that separately concatenated modules overlook. It also expands the claimed dataset contribution from 24,000+ to 50,000+ assets, without redefining the paper's overall objective.

C2.justification: New Section 5 identifies MPM computational cost and the synthetic-to-real gap, including simplified constitutive models, as deployment limitations. v2 retains the rigid-object generalization and uniform-material assumptions from v1, but removes the specific LGM/MVDream dependency limitation. It also adds explanations of failures caused by overly constrained video-generation prompts.

D1.justification: v2 substantially expands architecture, optimizer, precision, camera, rendering and evaluation specifications. It adds participant recruitment and filtering details, annotation prompts, numerical property mappings, and explicit trajectory-alignment instructions. Conversely, v1's 30/20 stage-epoch counts and 50% augmentation probabilities are no longer supplied. These are documentation changes in addition to the actual protocol revisions; the project-page access information remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion of trajectory-guided PhysCtrl and image-output-only LVSM, includes LIRM and Long-LRM, and updates technical attribution for its transformer, MVAdapter and Qwen-based pipeline. References to MVDream, SigLIP-2, DeepSDF and 4D-fy disappear. The broader positioning against physics-agnostic generation and slow per-scene optimization remains, so this is an extension of the literature context rather than a wholesale repositioning.

P1.justification: The abstract and substantial related-work and method passages are rewritten, with the probabilistic-modeling narrative replaced by a structured architecture explanation. v2 introduces numbered main sections, a separate Discussion, and an appendix organized into implementation, constitutive models, dataset statistics, construction, results and limitations. References move from before the supplement to the end. These constitute substantial narrative and structural editing beyond added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 redraws the architecture diagram, moves the overview to the first page, adds a dataset-construction diagram and multi-view/reconstruction visualizations, and introduces reconstruction, comparison-summary, distribution and property-mapping tables. Figure 5 assembles examples already present in v1's appendix. The older qualitative figures are retained with changed placement and numbering, while the document's typography, captions and page layout are broadly reformatted.

improvement.justification: v2 addresses v1's limited reconstruction validation and sparse reproducibility information through the GSO benchmark and detailed appendices, and adds useful deployment limitations. However, its new user-study description names different comparators from Table 1, leaving the revised preference evidence ambiguous. Its new Table 5 counts also sum to 48,215 rather than the stated 50,215 objects. These inconsistencies affect important empirical and dataset specifications, so the benefits and reliability problems do not support a confident net quality judgment.
